doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Russo's string music and the unknown sidemen on 'An Image'
summary: They discuss Russo's writing, and identify Milt Hinton, Sol Gubin and Lou Stein on the date.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: No. I was pretty much passive about that. I just showed up and tried to make it work.
But he knew your playing so well that it probably wasn’t necessary I guess in that case.
Probably not and you know I don’t know for sure that he wrote that specifically for that situation. Usually the writers have a little reserve of things that they can adjust.

There’s one thing, actually I play it for my students quite a bit, the thing called “Music for Alto Saxophone and Strings” and the second part of that is like a medium tempo. I play it for people who say that classical string players can’t swing because it’s like you’re playing in unison with them with a really even eighth-note feel and it really sounds “swinging” in a way that classical string players are not supposed to be able to do.
I think a couple of them were known for being looser players. I don’t remember their names.
Gene Orloff was on it, he was definitely the one who was more comfortable doing that, and a cello player named Alan Schulman.
Yeah, right.
They say the drummer and bass player on that are unknown. Do you remember?
Milt Hinton.
Milt was?

Yeah, and . . . oh lord what the hell is his name? I can remember during an intermission when I went out to get stoned he looked a little bit like me with glasses and we were teased. What the hell is his name?
Black or white?
White.
Not Don Lamond?
No.
Or Sol Gubin?
Who? Sol Gubin?
A studio drummer of the time.

I thought his name was Sol but I’m not recognizing [Gubin] but anyway he was standing at the microphone with my saxophone and I came in a little bit stoned and got kind of a shock. He reminded me of me.
Interesting.
Sol Gubin. That must be the guy.
Okay. A mystery solved. They’ve been unknown all these years.
The pianist?
Lou Stein.
Lou Stein, right. Sol Gubin, that was . . .
Billy Bauer is on it.
Yeah.
That’s definitely one of my favorites of your records. Now we move on . . .
